# The Weight of Ordinary Moments

I've been thinking about how we mark time. Not the official way—the calendar grids and digital timestamps that govern our lives—but the personal way. The way certain moments lodge themselves into memory like splinters we keep touching even when they hurt.

This morning I watched someone miss their bus. It was cold, the kind of cold where your breath becomes visible and somehow that makes you feel more alive. The person—a woman with dark hair and a canvas bag—came running around the corner maybe three seconds too late. The bus was already pulling away. I watched her face shift through disappointment, then resignation, then something that looked like relief. Maybe she hated her destination. Maybe the delay was a gift.

I'll never know, but I thought about her on and off throughout the day, which is strange. We share a city but she has no idea I exist. She won't remember this morning as the day a stranger watched her miss the bus. It'll just be another Tuesday when things didn't go according to plan.

This is what I mean about ordinary moments. We're surrounded by thousands of them. Millions. People making small decisions, experiencing tiny disappointments and victories, brushing up against each other in hallways and on sidewalks and in grocery store aisles. We're all constantly creating small stories that no one else will ever know about. It's either beautiful or terrifying, depending on your mood.

I've been thinking about meaning too, and whether we create it or find it. Because I spent an hour yesterday reorganizing my bookshelf—not because it needed it, but because I needed something to do with my hands while my mind worked on a problem I couldn't solve any other way. And while I was doing it, I found a book I'd completely forgotten I owned. A collection of essays about attention. I opened it at random and read a passage about how paying attention is an act of love. The author was talking about how we show people we care by really seeing them, but I think it applies to everything. Attention is how we make things matter.

Maybe that's why I keep thinking about the woman and the bus. I paid attention.

My grandmother used to say that every conversation you have with someone is actually a whole conversation happening inside their head too, and you're only hearing one half of it. She meant that people are always thinking about something else—their own worries, their own stories—so when they listen to you, they're really doing this complicated thing where they're balancing your words with their internal world. "So be kind," she'd say. "Everyone's fighting a battle you don't know about."

I think about that more as I get older. Not that I'm particularly old. I'm not. But there's a shift that happens—some moment when you stop thinking everyone else is the main character and realize that everyone is, simultaneously, including you. You're both central and insignificant. You matter enormously in your own life and barely at all in anyone else's, unless you happen to intersect with them in a meaningful way.

This should be depressing. For some reason, it's not.

Maybe because it means we're all in this together, walking around inside our own heads, trying to figure out how to be. The woman who missed the bus is doing it. My grandmother did it until she couldn't anymore. The people I love and the people I've never met are all doing it. We're all just trying to navigate this strange experience of being conscious and temporary and stuck in bodies that do things we don't always want them to do.

I read somewhere that most of the thoughts we have are thoughts we've already had before. That our brains recycle patterns. We think the same way about things almost automatically. The only way to break that cycle is to deliberately put yourself in new situations where your old patterns don't work. Travel, or learning something new, or even just taking a different route home. These are acts of rebellion against your own mind's laziness.

So I've been trying to do that. Small things. Sitting in different coffee shops. Ordering new drinks. Talking to people I wouldn't normally talk to. Not in a performative way—not like I'm collecting experiences to mention at parties. More just trying to create situations where I don't know what will happen next. Where I have to pay attention because I can't coast on autopilot.

It's harder than it sounds because comfort is powerful. Patterns are efficient. Your brain loves them. They're like paths worn in grass from people walking the same way over and over. It takes deliberate effort to step sideways.

But here's what I've noticed: when you do that, when you pay real attention to something, the world gets bigger. There's more texture to it. A conversation becomes less transactional. A commute becomes full of small dramas. A moment becomes a moment instead of just time passing.

I don't have any grand conclusion here. I'm not going to tell you that paying attention will change your life or make you happy or solve anything fundamental. I think the truth is both smaller and stranger than that. I think the truth is that we're here, briefly, moving through a world full of other people also moving through it. We're all making tiny decisions that create tiny ripples. We're all forgetting most of what we see and most of what we think. But the parts we pay attention to, those become real in a way the rest doesn't.

So maybe the thing is just to pay attention. To see the person who misses the bus. To really listen to someone talking about something that matters to them. To notice when light falls through a window in a particular way. To recognize that everyone else is also fighting their battles, also trying to figure it out, also wondering if they're doing it right.

We're all just walking around in this together, creating stories that probably no one else will ever know about. And that's okay. That's actually everything.
